utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, this witness has asked for no protection. It's been fully explained to him that those options could be open to him, and he's quite happy to testify in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you mind, Mr. Smith? I'm sorry, I apologise, but I understand Mr. McGreeghan is here, and probably even for you it's better to start at 2.00 and now we could spend the next few minutes discussing this matter. I apologise. Thank you. Is it in closed session? No, because we are not going to mention any name. Most of this trial is in closed session; it's a pity for the public -- I mean, for the idea of a fair and public trial. We are very keen on a public trial. It's a basic notion of international criminal justice. Now, I understand Mr. McGreeghan is the deputy head of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McGreeghan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You are sitting there not as a witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am grateful to you for coming here. I wanted to ask you to report on the conditions of Witness SA --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: Yes. I received this morning, as you're aware, a fax from a member of my staff. At the moment, I'm acting as deputy coordinator of the unit, Mr. Bauduin being elsewhere, and this morning I received a fax from our field office in Sarajevo, from Ms. Wendy Lobwein. Do you want me to relate all the content of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe you could summarise the content because this document has been circulated to both parties and also the Court was given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: As soon as I received the document, I read it several times, and I think it does become apparent that since the witness was last here in The Hague, her condition has deteriorated. She is receiving treatment in the region. The treatment is referred to in the report of Ms. Lobwein, and I'm satisfied from the report -- I'm not sure what Your Honours' decision will be -- but I'm satisfied from the report that at this time the witness isn't in a condition to travel or to appear before the Court. I have that very clear impression from the report of Wendy Lobwein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from -- I wonder whether the parties would like to ask questions of Mr. McGreeghan. Yes? Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I would kindly ask you: Was there any kind of insight made to the medical documentation pertaining to that witness, because from the report, we cannot see that the medical documentation has indeed been reviewed, and the person who has signed the report is obviously not a physician. Therefore, I simply wish to know whether this is a personal subjective assessment of the medical condition of the witness, or has there been any analysis, any review, examination of the medical documentation that's been made, and what are the qualifications of the person who conducted the interview with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: The interview with the witness was conducted by Wendy Lobwein. She has been a member of the staff in the Victims and Witnesses Unit since October 1995. Her training in university in Australia resulted in her receiving a bachelor of social work from the University of Queensland, and in the intervening period between then and now, she has dealt extensively with cases of trauma resulting from war situations and has, as I understand, a number of publications printed in relation to this work. She is widely experienced and recognised for her care in the treatment of witnesses of traumatic events. As far as a review of the medical documentation, that has not been carried out by anyone on my staff. There's no one suitably qualified to carry out an assessment of such documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes? Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: A week ago, I think it was last week or the week before, that we received documentation relating to the tests that were performed on the witness, and according to that medical documentation, we are dealing with a person who is healthy. She did not suffer -- I mean, there was no diagnosis of any physical problems. So according to the documents, we are dealing with a healthy person. This is the first time that we hear something like this. The person who conducted the interview also offered a medical diagnosis, and she stated that we are dealing with a case of post-traumatic stress disorder, it's a real illness, a psychiatric illness, psychological illness. So it seems to me that it is very difficult for someone who is not fully qualified to offer this kind of diagnosis, notwithstanding the experience, work experience, of the person who was in charge of conducting the interview. This particular illness is a very serious disorder, and this is what we concluded on the basis of the documents that were given to us last week; and therefore, we have two completely different reports: We have a report from the physician and a report from the social worker which differ a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have not had sight of the documents referred to from the previous medical examination, so I can't comment on that examination. But as a layman, I can foresee quite a difference in someone being physically healthy and yet having a fear of recall of the situation as this witness will testify -- or should that witness testify before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No questions of Mr. McGreeghan, but I remind you that we do have some time ahead of us when it comes to this witness because it is a witness summoned by the Trial Chamber, and that person could be summoned until the end of December or the beginning of January, so we're not really pressed -- you know, we're not under time pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excellent idea. I thought of that myself. You may remember that we decided to summon this lady as a Court witness; however, without going so far as to subpoena her. Now, we fully trust the competence and the experience of the various members of the Victims and Witnesses Unit who have been dealing with this particular lady, and we feel that it is probably not necessary now to insist to call her as a witness. However, we decide to admit into evidence her three written statements, so that they will be part of the evidence of this Tribunal. I don't know whether this -- what sort of evidence ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Court exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Court Exhibits will be C? C-1? Anyway, they will be taken into account as evidence before the Tribunal, but I think there is no point in insisting -- although I very much appreciate the suggestion made by the Prosecution that we have a lot of time. She could be, in theory, called later on when the Defence case starts and during the Defence case. But I think, judging from also the relevance and importance of the evidence, it may be sufficient, as I say, to admit those three statements into evidence. So it is so decided, and we can now adjourn, and we will -- again, thank you, Mr. McGreeghan, so much for your cooperation, and let me once again express the deep appreciation of this Tribunal for the excellent work and extremely professional work you are doing on behalf of victims and witnesses. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCGREEGHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, but I forgot to offer into evidence the statement of the previous witness, the statement that she gave to the Prosecutor, that it should be part of the record, that and Exhibit 263, but the other version where she indicated the location where the group of soldiers was. This exhibit has already been marked as Exhibit 263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On the same issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No objection whatsoever to the request made by Mr. Susak, but I didn't quite get which statement he was speaking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The one dated March 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The statement dated 5th and the 15th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. No objection. And also the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And also the photograph but with the marking --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, that it be part of the record as a separate exhibit, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will be D5/4, and the photograph is marked D6/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That is the same photograph which had already been offered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will make a copy of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excellent. All right. It is so decided, so it will be admitted into evidence. We adjourn now until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon. I just wanted to say something with regard to the witness that we discussed before, who is a witness of the Court. And I would just -- SA, and to say that we received six statements. Mr. President, you said that there were three statements which would be adopted. So we don't know whether you have received everything from the Prosecutor, everything that we have received was from the Prosecutor's office, and I do not -- I do want all six statements to be on the list. I don't know whether we should make a copy of what we have received, the documents we have received, because the Prosecution abridged the statements on several occasions, and I don't know if you have the integral text of the statements. That is to say, whether you have all the texts and all the integral texts. So I don't know how we should decide in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's very easy. You are right, we should admit into evidence all the statements you have received, and we will ask the Prosecution to double-check. I will also check my own file, and if some documents are missing I'm sure the Prosecution will be kind enough to give us all the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more point linked with that witness. The Trial Chamber has decided to accept the evidence and not to call the witness, but we do not know the importance of this statement, the last written proposal sent by the protection unit, Victim and Witnesses Protection Unit. As we're dealing with an individual who is suffering from post traumatic stress syndrome, we don't know how her statement will be assessed, whether it will be assessed by the statement -- by somebody suffering from a psychological disturbance, which could reduce the value of the statement. Let me go back to the fact that we do not have any relevant medical documentation with regard to this fact. So we should like to propose either to have medical expertise performed, or for that last document not to be taken into consideration. It is the last document that we obtained today from the Victim and Witnesses Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You mean this report, the one we got today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, this will not be taken into account, only the statements, the six -- did you mention six statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, six. Prosecutor, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Kablar. How are you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and I say good afternoon to all of you in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In 1993 you lived in the town of Vitez. Can you explain to the Court who you lived with, and what your job was and what life was like early in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: My name is Zaim Kablar. I was born on the 26th of June, 1957 in Vitez. I'm a Bosnian and have two children, girls. I worked in Vitez in the Vintizit Vitez Work Organisation. That's where I was born and that's where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were employed as a financial advisor or an economist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Of late I worked as the sales purchasing manager in the work organisation, for the past three years that is. Before that I worked in the financial department and commercial department, and I started off by works as a statistics expert, plan and analysis, the department for plan and analysis, but I have been working in Sintevit since 1986. I worked there up until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In April 1993 you were in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, what were you doing during the day?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, I was doing my regular duties at the -- in my work organisation, from 7.00 to 3.00 every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Previously that month had you been somewhere? Had you visited Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I -- on the 3rd of April, up till the 13th of April, I went to Maribor on business. I visited several firms with my colleague working in the commercial department with me, Mr. Ruzic. We went to Vetotechna (phoen) and visited a number of companies there. We returned on the 13th of April, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, can you tell the Court what happened, what you first saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, as my work begins at 7.00, I got up at half past five, started getting ready to go to work at quarter to six. Detonations were heard and shooting was heard, and I saw that something was wrong. I saw that -- I just waited to see what was going to happen, in fact. In the meantime, the neighbour living up above me came down to my flat, Mr. Mijo Ruzic. He came down. We saw that something was happening, and between 9:00 and 10.00 a.m. we were in my flat on the second floor, and on the third floor is where my neighbour who had been with me on the business trip to Slovenia lived, and we saw across the road that there was a Kombi parked there and that people were being taken away. As I saw that they were Muslims, I saw that they were getting Gerin Muazem away. I saw that something was happening. Then we went up to the third floor to Mijo's flat and I stayed there. On the 16th I spent the night there and then returned to my flat on the 17th. In the meantime, while I was in my own flat, I noticed, as I'm on the second floor, in the Banjalucanka building, that's the name of my building, I can see down the road, next to my building was the Vitezanka building, and I saw the hairdressing salon owned by Zume Lasovic, I think that this was on fire, and shooting could be heard. We spent the night in Mijo's place and we stayed there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think you said that you saw some Muslims being taken away. Who was taking the Muslims away and what type of people were these Muslims? Were they male, female, women, children?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I already said that they were taking Muazem away. There was a Kombi, and they took Gerin away. His flat is in the first entrance of our building. I think it was Hadja's brother. I don't know the name exactly. I saw that they were collecting Muslims, and so I went up to Mijo to see what was going to happen, because I didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who were the people taking these Muslims away? What military group did they belong to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms, and they could have been none other than the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once you saw these people being arrested and during that day seeing the hairdressing salon on fire --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Between 9.00 and 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's when the arrests were taking place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No. First of all, the salon was on fire between 9.00 and 10.00 and they were taken away after that. I suppose that -- in fact, the hairdressing salon, there is the hairdressing salon and then Smaija's house and then there was shooting and probably some fighting, and after that there was a settling of accounts, and the hairdressing salon was then set fire to. I couldn't see any further because I couldn't see from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stayed at Mijo Ruzic's house overnight; is that correct? On the night of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It's a flat. It's not a house, it's a flat. I'm on the second floor, he is on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What were you doing in the apartment? You were hiding; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I didn't have to hide there. In my entrance there were eight apartments. The Muslims and I went up to the third floor, and Sejo went over to Mijo and that's where we were. Had I known what was to have happened, I would have left on the 16th and not waited until the 19th because it was better for safety reasons to leave than stay, but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the Saturday did you move back to your apartment, the day after you heard the shooting and explosions?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, the next day, because there was a lot of propaganda via Radio Vitez, and they said that if anybody was harbouring Mujahedeen that they would be put up before a firing squad. Now who they thought of, probably not the section of town -- there were no Mujahedeen there and no Muslim army there, just apartment blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you hid in your apartment for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The 17th and 18th. On the 19th in the afternoon, at 6.00, they came for me and I went like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say they came for you, who came and took you away?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Three men from the HVO police. There were Cicin, and there was a young man who worked with my wife and I didn't know the third. They came to fetch me and then Sejo, we were the only ones left. Everybody had left. A white Kombi was parked in front of the apartment building, and we were taken into it and taken to the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Before you were placed into the Kombi, did anything happen in the car park in relation to another HVO soldier -- or in relation to an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: In front there was a young soldier. I don't know what he -- he wanted to kill me with his rifle. I don't know -- I don't know. He cocked his rifle at me. I don't know what he wanted to do. He just cursed me, he swore at me, and I was in the entrance as they told me to be, and Cicin too. I told him to leave, and I went into the Kombi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many other men were arrested and placed in the Kombi?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Sejo, myself and two other men, I think. They were with us. But mostly everyone -- everything had already been completed on the 16th, and when I got to the cinema there were many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where was the cinema in relation to your apartment? How far away was it from your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Approximately 300, 400 metres. Not more. I lived in the Banjalucanka building. It there was 300, 400 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived at the cinema, about how many other people had been detained there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There were three locations in the cinema. Down in the boiler room. I was taken to the boiler room. Up above there were offices on the floor above, to the right. I couldn't tell you exactly how many there were there, I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the cinema? Who was in charge of the prisoners at the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which military group was controlling the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was the main commander in charge of the cinema in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Do you mean the police or do you mean the command of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, who appeared to be in charge at the cinema? Was there a particular personality that appeared to be making sure that everyone stayed there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I don't understand you once again. Do you mean the police of the HVO, the commander or somebody who kept records as to which people were brought to the cinema? If you have in mind the commander, it was Mario. He was the command of the brigade, and for the cinema there was Anto Kovac and Zalac. If you're thinking about the records, there was Boris Jovicic who wrote down our names. I don't know who you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that the cinema was controlled by the HVO, and which groups of the HVO controlled the cinema? I mean, in terms of police or brigades, civilian police or Military Police, or any other particular group.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The Military Police. And that was where the command of the Vitez brigade was. There was Mario Cerkez, Gerin Muazem. If you have a picture, I can show you exactly where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll show you two pictures now, and if you can explain them to the Court as to what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The aerial photograph is marked 267, and the other photograph is marked 268.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the Exhibit 268 -- sorry, just wait for a moment. Looking at the Exhibit 268, can you tell the Court what that is a picture of?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: This is the facility that we called Kena cinema, but it had the worker's university entitled Moshow Pijade. Here where the car stands -- I don't know if you can see what I'm showing you, what I'm indicating, this is the exit out of the cinema, of what we called the Kena. These pine trees, there was another exit out of the cinema itself, and this was where the command of the Vitez brigade was located. Planks were put on the windows for protection purposes, to stop somebody the shooting from Stari Vitez, because these two windows could be directly seen from there. I was here where the car is, down here. That's the boiler room. There were two rooms there, one smaller room. So there were, in fact, two rooms which were not hit. There was a boiler room down there to provide heating for the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was the commander in charge of the Military Police at the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there Military Police, HVO Military Police at the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was -- whether it was Anto Kovac, whether he was the head man or not, I don't know, but I saw that he was in charge, but I don't think he was at the head of the Military Police. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he belong to the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stayed in the cinema for about four or five days before you were taken somewhere else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where you were taken and who you were taken with?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It was on the 24th -- between the 24th and 25th. It was night, in the night. It was half past eleven and half past twelve p.m. A young man came. I think he was from Cajdras. Then he would point us out and say we would go. I said I had a stomach ache, but he said it didn't matter. There was a Kombi parked in front of the building of the regular type. That is, had there been a regular policeman inside I don't think this would have happened, but there were no regular policemen, there was this man. If it was somebody from Vitez I wouldn't have gone trench digging. I would have found my way somehow and I would have stayed there, which would have been normal because everybody would know me. Somebody else would have gone. But as I didn't know this young man I went in with this group and we into the Kombi and went in an unknown direction. Before that, for the five days I spent at the cinema there was no problem because they were all people from Vitez, so I had no problems. Nobody had any problems as far as that part is concerned, in the cinema itself. The accommodation wasn't that good in the cellar, but you could go up to the cinema itself, or up on the floor above. But I didn't want to, I stayed below, because if the building was shelled, who was in the cellar would stay alive, so that's why I chose that solution. It wasn't such a good solution lodging wise, accommodation wise, but safer. But I didn't have any bad treatment towards me. Nobody was maltreated in the cinema, nor was anybody killed. The food was not very good. We had visits by families; your wife could come, she could bring you something to eat, to drink. You could contact your friends, you could ask them to bring you something. So there wasn't any problem with regard to that aspect in the cinema. There were a lot of us, but well, I don't think it was so bad. And my opinion is that it was safer there than if we had stayed at home. That is my opinion it depends on your aspect -- how you saw things. Later on, it turned out that I was right, because -- let's go back to the 24th and 25th. We would be taken into the Kombi, we went in front of the cinema -- would you like me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can just stop there. About how many people were taken into the Kombi?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It was difficult for me to tell. I believe it was between 15 and 20 people. I was very frightened at that moment. I minded my own business. I didn't count anyone, and I wasn't really watching anyone. I was only thinking of myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these were Muslim --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: But I believe there were between 15 and 20 people. Yes, they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have a choice to go or were you ordered to go?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No, there was no choice whatsoever. People didn't know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you told that you were going trench digging; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Nobody told us anything. We had to go and we didn't know where we would stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said this was the night of the 24th and 25th of April. About what time did you leave the cinema and -- what time did you leave the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Half past eleven, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where was the first place you stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The first place where we stopped was at the Bungalow, and this is where we got off the Kombi, the van, and then we heard a very loud explosion. It was dark. It was past midnight at that time. So there was this very loud explosion, and a man suddenly appeared and he told us to squat behind the van. He was also frightened because he didn't know what was happening. There was this Bungalow, and behind the Bungalow, there was the forest, the woods. So when we heard the explosion, it was chaos because everybody was frightened all of a sudden, and the driver said, "Let us move on." So we got on the van again and we moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How far away was the explosion from the Bungalow, about?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Not very far from the Bungalow, maybe 50 or 100 metres away. At least that's how it seemed to me. It was difficult for me to orient myself, but it was very close because the soldiers were also afraid, not to mention ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many soldiers were with you when this explosion occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was the driver who was with us and two policemen, one had got out of the van, so I think that there were five or six of us in total. It was difficult for me to tell because it was dark, so I couldn't see very clearly who was standing where, and you couldn't really observe the situation. It's very difficult to have an idea as to how many people there were in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know if they were HVO military police or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was no police. The HVO -- you mean the people who came out of the wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The people who came with you in the Kombi.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, the police, two policemen, and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know which type of police they were: military or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was no civilian police. They were all HVO members. It was wartime. The civilians were no longer in the picture. You know, it was already war by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did someone seem to be in charge? Once the explosion had gone off, did someone appear to be in charge of the HVO at the Bungalow, did the police and any other HVO member you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: A man came out of the wood and he was making a lot of noise, and I suppose that he was in charge. Later on, we learned that he was in charge indeed. Later on, we can mention his name. Later on, it will become apparent -- I can mention his name as well. But at that time, I didn't know who that man was. It was only later, the next day, the following day, that I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if you mention that man's name now? and we understand that you only came to know of it later. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We know him by the nickname of Cicko and it is actually Miroslav Bralo, and later on he was in charge of the location where I went digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was he doing and what did he say when you were at the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: He shouted at us. He told us to squat, to put our hands behind our head, and then when things were a little bit quieter, he told the driver to move on. He said, "Drive on. Just go on." He said that to the driver. Maybe I didn't express myself very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You're expressing yourself very clearly. Can you give a description of this Miroslav Bralo, how tall he was, what colour his hair was, and his approximate age?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: You mean that night, that evening, or later on? That evening, I could not identify him. I couldn't see him very well. It was only later on when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you give the Court a description of him when you saw him later on?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes. He's a young man. My height is about one metre and eight -- seventy, and he's about 10 centimetres taller than me. He's not fat or anything. I used to know him by sight, but I didn't know him very well before that because he didn't -- he wasn't around in Vitez very often. I would only see him from time to time. Later on, I learned who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mention this place, the Bungalow. What village is that in?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The village of Nadioci. This is how we know that village, by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you look at the map behind you, would you be able to locate where the Bungalow was, just the general area? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Mm, here (indicating). This is the village of Nadioci. Somewhere near the main road, the road leading to Busovaca. It was on the right side of the road as you come from Vitez. The Bungalow is on the right side of the road. It's maybe five kilometres away from Vitez. It's not a very good picture. You can only see maybe two or three villages on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I show you a photograph now, will you tell the Court whether you can recognise that? I'm sorry, Your Honours. It's apparently in evidence already. Prosecution Exhibit 119.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: This is the Bungalow. This is quite clear, that it's the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you went to the Bungalow, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We went on. We continued, though we didn't know exactly where we were going. At one point, the lights were out in the van, but we reached Kaonik and then we turned right, and then we travelled maybe 200, 300 metres from Kaonik and reached some kind of hangar which was situated 100 metres away. Before the war, it used to be a JNA warehouse, a depot, part of the barracks. I don't know what it was called. The army used to be quartered there. So this is where we were left, near that hangar. I had never been there before, and I didn't even know where I was, so it was difficult for me to tell where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did you see when you arrived at the Bungalow? Sorry. What did you see when you arrived at Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: When we entered the hall, there was a guard there, and I knew that person. In a situation like that, it's good for you if you know someone, if there is someone you know, and this is someone I went to school with in Travnik, so it was easy for me to establish some kind of contact with him. So we entered this place, this facility, the hangar, and on the left side of the hangar, there were some people lying -- at first I thought they were dead -- they were lying down on some kind of pallets, and there was a fireplace in the hangar and we came close to the fireplace because we couldn't sleep at that moment. But in the morning, when people woke up, we realised that there were a number of people there, maybe 20 of them, and they were alive. I thought that the guard would be coming back to pick us up -- actually, I was hoping that he would show up so I could have some kind of contact with him and it would have been easier for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you told where these men had come from, what areas, what towns or villages?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I asked them. We kept asking each other, we wanted to know where people were from. Those were all elderly people from Jelinak, Loncari. There was also a couple of people who had been brought there -- who had been picked up in the street or on the road when the conflict broke out. There were only two or three of them who were not from Jelinak or Loncari. At that time, I didn't even know where Jelinak and Loncari were. It was only later on that I learned. I didn't move around a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to show you another photograph, and if you can explain to the Court what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph is marked 269.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: This is the main road to Busovaca, and there used to be a disco called Leptir here and I used to go there -- I used to go to this area, and this is the turnoff that leads to Kaonik, and then maybe 200, 300 metres away, we turned, and this is the area where we stopped. I believe that this is the hangar where I was placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I spent only that night there. On the following morning, the same driver came in the same van at about 10.00, and we were moved to another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We were taken -- I didn't know where we were. But at any rate, we were taken to Kuber. I wasn't quite certain of the name of the place at the beginning; I didn't know whether it was Kuber or Guber. It is not far from Loncari, that locality. It is called Kuber, and that is the first time that I had been there. The van remained some 200 metres away from that location, and we were taken to a house where some HVO soldiers were quartered, and as I say, I had never been there before and I wasn't aware of the name of the place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long did it take you to drive from Kaonik to this house?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Forty minutes, maximum, maybe up to one hour. Difficult to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned there were some HVO soldiers at this house. Do you remember any of them in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: When we got there in front of that house which was situated on the left-hand side, there was a shed near the house, and we sat there in front of the shed in a semicircle. Cicko came. There were a few other soldiers there. Then he forced us to make the sign of a cross. There was a young man who couldn't do it. I knew how to do it because I had worked in that area. I worked with a colleague, and I would go to a mosque -- and I also knew how to do that. Anyway, this young man was very frightened, and Cicko was about to hit him with a spade. I don't think that he would have killed him in front of us. But somehow eventually this young man managed to make the sign of a cross, and we remained there for a while, we were just sitting there. After a while, we were taken in the direction of Kuber. We were digging trenches. We stayed there until nightfall, until about 8.00. On that frontline, there were some of our people -- when I say "our people," I use it conditionally. I mean people who I knew from before, from the Kolonija neighbourhood. It's easier if there are people who are known to you; we were not really afraid because we were together. I was lucky because I didn't have to work very hard on this particular spot, but later on, I was moved to another spot where I had to dig. It all lasted until about dusk, until nightfall, when we were taken back to the same house. After that, we were taken to another location near the village of Vrhovine, and this is where we were taken care of by some other people who were not very nice, and we really had to work very, very hard. There were no breaks. We had to dig all the time, from 8.00 p.m. until 6.00 a.m. the next morning, without break. I was all wet, I was sweating, my clothes were completely wet. This is where I was sweating very hard and I got dry there. Later on they gave me some tea. There was this very young man with us who used to play football with me. He realised that I was feeling ill, and so he gave me some tablets. I took some tablets. We remained there for about ten hours. Then Cico, the driver, arrived, and I told him that I should be taken to see a doctor, that I was not feeling very well, and he said that he would see about that, and after half an hour, he came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but just so that the Court is not confused. You mentioned a Cicko, a person who was at the house when you first arrived to dig trenches, and is that Miroslav Bralo?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It's the same person, but he just has the nickname Cicko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Then you mentioned another, I think, Cico, who took you away or who was at the house when you were feeling sick. Is that a different person to Cicko?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It's a different person. He wasn't in the house; he was the driver and had brought something to the house. This was about 10.00 the next day. But it's a different person. It's the driver who drove the van and who took us up to the Bungalow and brought us back. It's the same person. I apologise. Let me just say that when we returned from Kaonik, he asked who I was and he knew who I was. He gave me a packet of cigarettes and I lit up a cigarette and then we went there. So if you knew somebody, you would have no problems. If you didn't know anybody, you would have problems. That's normal, I suppose. At least that's what I thought to be true. I used the people I knew, and if I didn't know anybody, well, tough luck. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could just ask you a few specific questions? Up until the moment that you mentioned that you were quite sick, you left Kaonik camp on Sunday morning, the 25th, and arrived at the house where Miroslav Bralo was and was forcing you to make signs of the cross about 12.00 on the 25th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you were sent away to dig some trenches and --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, to the right, towards Kuber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At that location, you had some guards that were quite friendly towards you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, to the right, towards Kuber. There were people from the colony. We call the area I lived in the colony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This area I think is Kolonija, that's the area that you lived in, and that's in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So these guards were from your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I didn't make --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Not the guards, the soldiers in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So at that first location where you were meant to dig trenches, you didn't have to dig too hard because you had your friends at that location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes. I was with the young man who had played in Vitez. I had played for Vitez too, and it would be stupid for me to dig trenches for him. He's younger than me. That's the situation that you make use of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you played soccer together?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You finished at that location, you finished being at that trench-digging location in the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts, because at around 6.00 p.m., there was a little fighting between Kuber and the other side, the Strane side, and then we went down towards the house from which we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why working at digging trenches, digging trenches is dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It's dangerous because you can be killed because you're right in front of one rifle and across the way from the other rifle, and you're digging in front of one and he can kill you. He's not interested in you. If you're digging here, then the other side can also get you, so you're up at the frontline, in fact, so both sides can kill you. You don't know where the wind's coming from, whether one side's going to kill you or the other side. Someone perhaps can know which side; some others don't. One of these people can send you up in front, and you can be killed from the other side. You don't know. That's the kind of situation it is. We call that a human shield. It is a human shield and it isn't a human shield. You can call it whatever you like. But it's something that is absolutely the most dangerous thing that you can imagine in this conflict. So it's an ordinary civilian making use of you sometimes and he can kill you. Perhaps somebody who knows you and doesn't like you can kill you, and then the other one can say, well, he killed me. They're all very -- the situation isn't good for the one in the middle, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The frontline, who was that between, which groups?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The frontline. Which military groups is that between?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The HVO was where I was. Over there, there was probably the army. I didn't see them. I didn't know who was there, but I suppose it was the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you arrived back after this trench-digging to the house at about 6.00 in the evening, and then you rested there for a while; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Then on the evening of the 25th, you went out trench-digging again to another location where the soldiers were not as nice to you as at the first location near Kuber or Guber?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was a drastic difference because the ones from Cajdras were here towards the Vrhovine side. They were dangerous. They would beat you up. You didn't know anybody there. But I had a little luck here because, as I say, there was this Crnogorac/Montenegrin digging with me, and somebody from a dugout recognised him and gave him some easier work to do, where I was wearing white sneakers and shot -- and so these are tricky situations. But it wasn't a good thing if you didn't know anybody. Had we known somebody, we could have had a rest perhaps, but as we didn't know anybody, I suffered the consequences drastically because I had never done any digging in my life, and I had to do a lot of digging and at night, and this Crnogorac -- this Montenegrin, never did any digging either and he had to dig, and we dug enormous trenches. Had someone told us to dig these trenches before the war, well ... But this was a situation when you had to, and we just dug them, and that's why I fell ill afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You dug trenches during the night, the night of the 25th and the morning of the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What time did you finish digging the trenches on the morning of the 26th, about what time?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: As soon as it was dawn because I suppose the frontline was close too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: But we dug some very good trenches, so you could move around safely. They were deep trenches, connecting trenches. We had done a good job. We fortified the area and then it was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it because you dug so well, that's why you got sick?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, I didn't dig too well, but I had a jacket on, and so I was ill when I had gone trench-digging, and then having dug the trenches, I felt even worse. I played active football for 25 years, and, of course, if your vest is wet from sweat and it dries on you, you'll be ill. Try it, you'll see. You will be ill straight off. And I had a vest and a pullover and a jacket, and everything was wet from the sweat from the work that I had been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got back to the house and you were feeling in this sick way -- this is in the morning of the 26th -- what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Nothing happened. I drank two cups of tea, I took two tablets -- I said that a moment ago -- and then the driver, Cico came, and as you couldn't communicate with Cicko, because I didn't know him and he wasn't fully conscious then, I would catch somebody that I knew. So I told him, "Listen, I want to get to a doctor." He left quickly and returned quickly and he said, "Well, let's go." So I went with him downhill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just before you went off with this Cico, who was in charge of the --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Cico.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Cico. Sorry about the accents, Your Honour. Before you went off with Cico, who was in charge of the HVO soldiers at the house where you went and dug trenches for?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was Cicko for that complete line, and I was afraid of him. They were afraid of him and we were afraid of him. Nobody had a good time of it there. The HVO soldiers were afraid of him and we were especially afraid of him. It was absolute chaos up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So Miroslav Bralo was in charge of that trench-digging operation on that part of the frontline; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: He was in charge of everything, for the soldiers and for us, and everything that moved up there was in his charge. The complete area was in his charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But you decided not to ask him to be released from trench-digging, you asked the driver?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No, it wasn't trench-digging, it was a pause, a break. What would have happened afterwards, I don't know. I just used the man, the driver who came, because the other one wouldn't let his mother escape from there if she was useful to him, so I used the man who came, the driver. I asked him to ask whether I could go to see a doctor, and I don't know what happened after that and what was to happen. He said, "Well, I'll see what I can do for you." He left and he came back about 45 minutes or one hour later. Where he went, I don't know. Later on, I was to learn where he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When he came back, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Nothing happened. He just said, "Let's go." And I left with him. I didn't report to anybody, I didn't say anything to anybody, we just left downwards, some 100 metres. We got into the van and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We stopped at the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how far away was that from the house where you were having a rest?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I've just told you. It's about half an hour away, perhaps less. It's difficult to orient yourself because you go through the wood, and then once you get to the road, there's only 20 metres. That is going down from the Bungalow where you turn off the road there. It's no problem. From the road to Kuber, I don't know how much that is. Nobody knows how far it is. I don't really know. You can't say exactly. But it's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened at the Bungalow? Did you see anyone there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We parked in front of the Bungalow. Cico got out, I got out. Vlado was sitting there, Vladimir Santic. He said "Hello"; we said "Hello." He said, "What's up, Zajko?" "Well," I just said, "I'm sick." He laughed, I laughed, and I continued on my way with the chauffeur to Vitez to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This is on the 26th of April. And Zajko, is that your nickname?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: That's what they call me. Somebody calls me Zajkica, Zajko Kabalar. Well, it's out of -- an affectionate nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a Vlado Santic. For about how long had you known this man?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I didn't get that. I didn't hear very well. Well, I've known him for a long time. We lived in the colony together. We're of the same age. He's of my generation. So everybody living around in the neighbourhood, everybody knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What job did he have before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: He was a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see him socially before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Never liked having policemen as friends. We were good friends. We would say hello, but we didn't socialise. I played soccer, and that was enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many times in a year would you see this Vlado Santic? Just on average, to give the Court an understanding of how well -- how able you were to recognise him before the war.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, we saw each other a hundred times. I'm 1.000 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: An investigator spoke to you before coming to the Tribunal and showed you 12 photographs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were asked to pick out -- if there was anyone in those photographs that you knew?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to pick out anyone in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, the photographs I was shown I pointed out Vlado. I don't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you remember what number was under his photograph? Each photograph had a number either above or below it. Do you remember what number that was?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: How do you mean, what number or what? What dress he wore?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking whether you can remember the number that Vlado Santic appeared --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: What number he was under. Number 6. Left half.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I show you these two exhibits now, can you tell the Court what they are?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you like to have these photographs marked as one exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 270.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Is this ordinary water or mineral water?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It would be flat if it was mineral water anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's ordinary water.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I don't know what you drink. You can drink what you like. I don't know what side you're on and what you drink. I don't know who's where. What do you want me to point out now? Number 6 is Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just ask that exhibit number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you look at the other page underneath the page with the number 6 on it. Does Vlado Santic appear on the other page, from 7 to 12?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No, it doesn't look at all like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you see Mr. Santic in court today, Vlado Santic, the man that was at the Bungalow on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but he's lost a little weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you point him out to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can. It's better for him to get up rather than me get up. Does it matter whether I come or he comes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which row is he on? He's on the second row of the court, on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There, he is. The man's got a lot of hair on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You're referring to the bald man in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I like playing jokes now and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I ask it be noted on the record that he identified Vladimir Santic. You said that he greeted you when you arrived at the Bungalow, and he said something like, "What's the matter, Zajko;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, something like the kind, yes. "What's up?" because I was moaning and I was ill, and when you see somebody you know, you feel better already and then you carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was he doing? Was he standing, sitting?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: He was sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you say anything to him when he asked you what was the matter?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, he asked me, "What's the matter?" And I said, "I'm a little ill." Nothing special. We didn't say anything special, and since we know one another, there were no problems there. Had we not known each other, I probably wouldn't have even got to that point. I probably would have stayed up there, because when the driver came he probably have said that it was me who was ill, and as he knows me, then he sent a car for me. Had he not known me as being a good man, I would have stayed up there, and it was very dubious whether I would have been brought down at all. I never said thank you to him, so I can say thank you to him now for sending the car to come and fetch me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who do you think was at a higher level in the -- I withdraw that question. What was he wearing, Vlado Santic, on this day, the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: As he was sitting down, he had a camouflage shirt on, a slightly better on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he have any patches on at all? Did you notice?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: They all had patches of the HVO. Very few of them didn't. It was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Vladimir Santic have patches on his uniform that day?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, on the left-hand side. Did you have them only the right -- on the left side? I beg your pardon. Yes, he did, on the left. He's not going to have it on the right arm. I had my on -- my patches on the left. We all had them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Miroslav Bralo, was he in uniform on that day, the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Oh, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: He never took it off. He never took off his camouflage uniform. He never took a uniform on -- he had a good uniform, it was a nice new uniform, and he didn't like to take it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you remember what type of uniform that was, what colour?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform. Not a very good one. Not like Vlado. Vlado had Napovka (phoen) NATO type.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Miroslav Bralo had any patches on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, yes. He would put -- place two patches on, not one but two, if he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what those patches said? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: "HVO." They all had HVO patches. Only the black ones, they had other patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, do you know what part of the HVO Vladimir Santic belonged to, whether it was the brigade, the Military Police or any other unit in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I don't really understand these different formations and who belonged to whom. He didn't belong to the army, that's for sure. He probably belonged -- he belonged to the HVO, but which unit I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say the army, you mean the Muslim army, the Bosnian army, the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know which group Miroslav Bralo may have belonged to within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. I was in such a situation I -- that I couldn't pay much attention to which unit people belonged. I only cared about getting safely to Vitez. I wasn't interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said that both Vladimir Santic and Miroslav Bralo were both in the HVO because of the patches you saw on their uniform, or that's what you presumed. Can you tell the Court which one you felt was at a higher level, Miroslav Bralo or Vladimir Santic? Are you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The one who had only four grades of elementary school could not have been higher than the other one. This other guy was only used to scare people away, and the other was a commander. He was sitting far from the frontline, ten kilometres from the frontline. We all know where commanders stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said the person that had the four grades of school, who was that Miroslav Bralo or Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Cicko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's Miroslav Bralo.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: (No audible response).

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You believed that Vladimir Santic was some sort of commander, is that correct, within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: He was always a commander. He always had a very good rating. No. Let us put all jokes aside. Cicko couldn't have been a commander at the frontline, because had Cicko had been commander, he wouldn't have let me leave that locality. He didn't let anyone go. When Cicko went to ask someone, he went to see Vlado, which was perfectly normal. Later on it turned out it was Vlado. We all knew who was in charge, it was not a secret, because we all knew each other in Vitez. It was not a big secret. If there's anyone who doesn't know me, it means that he's not from Vitez. It's not much of a secret. People knew what other people did. There was no problem. If Cicko had been in charge, I would have never left that place, but that person knew me, and that person approved my going to see a doctor. It was some sort of mitigating circumstance. It's nothing -- nothing really bad at that moment, as far as I'm concerned. As to what happened later on, it's really none of my business. There are other people who will take care of that. But that was the person who helped me at that moment. If I hadn't seen him, I wouldn't have come here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just to be clear, your evidence is that Vladimir Santic approved you to go and have leave from trench digging; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that to be correct, because when we reached the parking area, I went to report to Vlado, and when he saw him, there was no problem. As far as trench digging is concerned, there were no records. Vlado didn't dispose of any kind of records as to who went trench digging. We were taken away by night. There were no lists of who had to go trench digging. Had Vlado known that I was there, maybe I wouldn't have stayed there at all, let other people dig. Just an example I'm giving. Because there was no record that was kept by the HVO. We were usually taken around midnight, when everybody was asleep, Vlado, Mario and others. Only the thugs would appear and they would take us away. There were no records that were being regularly kept. People didn't know that we were there. So in that regard, I was lucky that things turned out that way for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned Miroslav Bralo and how you were told by other people that this person that you saw at this Bungalow on the occasion that you went to Kaonik camp --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Could I have the volume turned up a little bit, please? This one -- I cannot hear this one very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No. Let's replace that. The other woman speaks very nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear the translator?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Now it's okay, even too good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were told that this person was called Miroslav Bralo?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Turn him down a little bit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who told you that, that he was Miroslav Bralo?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: While we were sitting there, when we arrived at that location, there were some HVO soldiers there, and there were also some of our people who knew him, because I would have introduced myself. I thought it was some kind of joke when he forced us to make a sign of the cross. I knew he was not crazy, but I thought that we better keep silent and let's see how things will turn. There were some other football players, I mean, people who used to play soccer with me before that, and we were discussing who he was, and at that point I learned who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you were told who he was, had you also been told that he was involved in a significant event earlier in 1993, an incident, a killing?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was in '93, but everybody knew, in Vitez, that he had tied a man to the bed and blew him up, and he was gone. Everybody knew that in Vitez. Only I didn't know who that person was. And it was up there at the location that I learned about him, and I just kept silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know the man's name who was blown up?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I think he was a shopkeeper. I think that Vlado would know his name, because he worked at the MUP. I believe it was Eso. Was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what village he lived?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It happened down there in the area of Santici or Nadioci. I don't know exactly where, but in the lower area, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go back to when you were allowed to go and see a doctor. Were you subsequently given a sickness certificate by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: They wrote a prescription for me, which also indicated that I should be spared from work, and I made that prescription available to you. I had to be spared from work for three days, and there was supposed to be a check-up on the 28th. That was at the health centre in our town. It was some kind of infirmary. Muhamed was there, Bosko was there as well. We had a kind of mini hospital there, and Muhamed examined me. He's a Muslim, and Bosko was a Serb. So it was valid. I mean, the prescription was valid and I had to be spared from work for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were given a certificate -- sorry for interrupting. You were given a sickness certificate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: To a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've spent about five minutes on this. Let's produce the certificate and let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll just produce a certificate, and if you tell the court if, in fact, that's a copy of the one that you received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 271.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is the certificate with the prescription for medicine. I can't read very well the doctor's handwriting. I got something for my stomach. You can also see that I was to be spared from work from the 26th to the 28th of April, and on the 28th I was returned to Vitez. Bosko signed the paper and Muhamed did too. Dr. Muhamed is a much better doctor than Bosko. Bosko's not much of a physician, but Muhamed, he's the real physician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is there an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There is no English translation at this stage, Your Honour, but one can be supplied and tendered at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After receiving that sickness certificate you went back to the cinema; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Then you were released on the 30th of April from the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We were released -- I mean, not all of us. At that time I thought that we would all be released. There was a cease-fire there, and the exchange took place on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you went back to your apartment and subsequently left Vitez one or two days later, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why did you leave Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Because it was not such a good idea to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For what reason? Why didn't you think it was a good idea to stay?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Because it was worse to be in an apartment than in the cinema. If you stayed at your apartment you could be taken away any day, any night, and if you have a family, you risk too much. That's how I decided, in view of the situation, which was not very good, and especially in view of the fact that I had a very nasty neighbour on the third floor, I thought I could be killed any time, so I decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you moved back to Vitez since?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you moved back to live in Vitez since you left in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Nobody returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will break now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I omitted to tender the documents, 267, 268, 269, and 271 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be cross-examining the witness. I only have a few brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I will be followed by Counsel Radovic and then by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Petar Pavkovic. I am Defence counsel for Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Pleased to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I will be brief. I will try to clarify certain things. You mentioned several times today that it was very important to know someone during those difficult times.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm waiting for the question to be translated. I'm afraid I'm not --

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: What do we need an interpreter for? You and I can understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but others have to follow us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any indication that other people can hear us as well. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So we understand each other. It was very important during those times to know someone. It was more important than anything else.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: It was also some sort of guarantee that you would be able to save your head. Could you please say it? Could you state your opinion in answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, that proved to be true in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I hope we can understand each other. We speak more or less the same language.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, it meant a lot in my case. In view of the location where I was, that was important. It was important to know someone. I didn't know that Vlado was there at the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that we will discuss later on. But tell me, when you met Vlado, at that point, you were quite satisfied, you were pleased to see him?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the danger you were exposed to while digging trenches, danger that came from both sides.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: That was my impression. That's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your encounter with Cicko and your experience with digging trenches, it was a relief for you to see Vlado.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, when I saw him, it meant that I could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Vlado let you go, that he spared you from digging trenches, and that he also saved you, saved your life; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Because I heard you say thank you to Vlado. You haven't had the opportunity to do so so far.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, because people were getting killed by trench-digging. I'm sure there are documents about that. There were a lot of casualties while digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So when Vlado referred you to someone else, to somewhere else, it meant that you were saved?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the way I understood. You stated explicitly. You thanked him for that.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about a person by the name of Cicko. You said few good things about him in the way you spoke.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, I knew him. I knew what kind of history he had, and I told you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
